column2: Dropping objects into a box, imitation games with spoon and cup, pointing to objects in pictures.
First steps may come (anywhere from 9 to 18 months is normal). 1–3 meaningful words, waving, pointing. Tries to use a spoon on their own.
A safe space for walking, simple shape sorting, songs and books together. Go to the 1-year check-up.
Walks a few steps; tries stacking objects. Recognises familiar people by name.
Stacking two blocks, scribbling with a chunky crayon (supervised), simple hide-and-seek games.
Walks more confidently; squats and stands up. Vocabulary grows; follows instructions like "give it to me".
Pushing a ball forward, nesting cups, "where is…?" questions with a picture book.
May crawl up stairs; learns to drink from a cup. Imitation play increases.
Talking on a toy phone, pretend play like feeding a doll, walks outdoors.
May walk backwards; stacks 3–4 blocks. Points to a few body parts.
Where's your nose? game, sand and water play (supervised), simple puzzles.
About 6–10 words; understands simple instructions. Better with a spoon; stubbornness may begin.
Offering choices ("apple or banana?"), shape sorters, tidying up together as a game.
Tries to run; climbs stairs with help. Points to objects in pictures, feeds a toy doll.
Let them turn pages while reading, big building blocks, dancing and music.
Vocabulary grows fast; some children start putting two words together.
Small tasks in daily routines ("bring your shoes"), colouring, finger rhymes.
Tries to kick a ball; use of spoon and fork improves. More interest in other children, but usually plays alongside them.
Ball games, simple sorting (big–small), play dough (supervised).
The wish to express themselves grows; tantrums may happen. Understands simple questions.
Naming feelings ("are you angry?"), role play, climbing outdoors (low and safe).
Goes up and down stairs holding on; scribbles are more controlled. A sense of ownership ("mine") becomes clear.
Turn-taking games, bucket and spade, telling a story together.
Two-word sentences become common; around 50 words is normal. Imitation and pretend play increase.
Toy kitchen, dressing up, simple counting songs.
Two years: runs, throws a ball, makes 2–3-word sentences, follows simple two-step instructions. Signs of readiness for potty training may appear.
Puzzles, colouring, ball games, reading books. Outdoor play instead of screens.
2–3 years: sentences get longer, starts learning colours and shapes, lots of "why?" questions. Tries dressing independently.
Pretend play, puzzles, play dough, tricycle, cooking together.
3–4 years: tells stories, can wait for a turn, starts playing together with friends. Stands on one foot briefly.
Simple games with rules, cutting with child scissors, dancing, nature walks.
4–5 years: interest in letters and numbers, tries to write their name, complex sentences. Starts putting feelings into words.
Board games, role play, gardening, library visits.
5–6 years: getting ready for school; attention span grows, understands games with rules, may learn to tie shoelaces.
Memory games, skipping rope, bike with stabilisers, reading together and asking questions.

Exclusive breast milk is recommended for the first 6 months; water, sugar water or herbal tea are not needed. If breast milk isn't enough, discuss formula with your paediatrician. Feed whenever your baby shows hunger cues (8–12 times a day).

If there are signs of readiness, start solid foods: one at a time, a few days apart, as purées. Iron-rich foods (meat, egg yolk, lentils) come first. No salt, sugar or honey is added; breastfeeding continues.

2–3 solid meals a day; gradually move the texture on to mashed and soft pieces. Introduce drinking water from a cup. You can introduce allergenic foods (egg, thinned peanut butter) appropriately; for at-risk babies ask a doctor.
3 meals and 1–2 snacks a day; soft finger foods. Foods that are a choking risk such as whole grapes and whole nuts are not given. No honey before 12 months; cow's milk is not given as the main drink.

Join family meals with low salt and an age-appropriate texture. 3 meals + 2 snacks a day. Daily milk should not exceed about 2 glasses. Breastfeeding can continue as wished. Picky eating is normal at this age.
Offer variety from vegetables, fruit, whole grains, protein and dairy. You decide what is eaten; the child decides how much. Limit sugary drinks and packaged snacks.
About 14–17 hours a day in short blocks is normal. On the back for every sleep, on a flat, firm surface; no pillows, duvets or toys in the cot. For the first 6 months, same room, separate bed.
About 12–16 hours a day (including daytime naps). Night waking may continue. An evening routine (bath, feed, lullaby) and putting down drowsy but awake help.
About 11–14 hours a day; daytime naps usually drop to one. A regular bedtime and a screen-free evening routine are important.
About 10–13 hours a day (including naps). Daytime naps are usually dropped between 3 and 5 years. Turn off screens 1 hour before bed.
In the first days after birth, heel-prick and hearing screenings are done; a first check-up is recommended on day 3–5.
Family doctor follow-up: assessment of weight gain, jaundice, belly button and feeding.
Family doctor follow-up and vaccines. Vitamin D should be given regularly; iron supplements start at 4 months (the dose is set by the doctor).
Developmental assessment; iron supplements continue.
1-year check-up: assessment of growth, development, anaemia and teeth.
Development and speech assessment; dental check-up.
Measure growth regularly and record it in the app; share your concerns with your family doctor.
Never leave your baby alone on a high surface, even for a moment; don't shake. Use a rear-facing car seat. Fever in a baby under 3 months needs urgent assessment.
Now that rolling has started, keep a hand on your baby on the changing table. Keep small objects, button batteries and cords out of reach.
Crawling and pulling-up stage: socket covers, stair gates, corner guards, fixing furniture to the wall. Don't use a baby walker.
Keep medicines and cleaning products in a locked cupboard; in case of poisoning call your poison control centre. Keep hot drinks and pan handles out of reach. Stay within arm's reach near water.
Window and balcony locks, holding hands on the street, an age-appropriate car seat. Teach your child their full name and the emergency number.

Observe everyday words, gestures, movement and self-care attempts through play.
Try simple two-step instructions, pretend play and social interaction together.
Give chances for storytelling, waiting for turns, movement coordination and naming feelings.
Support asking questions, solving problems together, drawing and friendship skills.
Support preschool skills with everyday responsibilities, storytelling, and number and sound games.
At this stage the basis of nutrition is breast milk or suitable infant formula. Follow your health professional's advice on solids, water and feeding changes.
Offer solids suited to developmental readiness in a safe texture; breast milk or suitable formula continues. Watch for allergy signs with new foods. Don't give honey.
Offer regular meals and snacks; respect hunger and fullness cues. Prepare grapes, hard nuts and similar choking risks appropriately.
Provide variety in vegetables, fruit, protein and grains. Involve your child in food preparation with age-appropriate tasks; avoid forcing them to eat.
Put your baby on their back for every sleep; no pillows, toys or loose covers on a flat, firm sleep surface. Sleep duration varies between babies.
Create a consistent evening routine. Watch changes in naps and night sleep; don't force a single target time.
Set a calm bedtime routine, a regular wake-up time and age-appropriate screen limits. Discuss prolonged sleep problems with a specialist.
While awake, try short supervised tummy play, talking and face-to-face interaction; take a break when they show signs of tiredness.
Play with soft sounds, reaching for safe objects and singing together.
Try peekaboo, hiding objects, picture books and movement games in a safe place.
Offer stacking blocks, imitation, picture books, simple rhythm and free movement play.
Try sorting, large-piece puzzles, a pretend kitchen and an obstacle course, with supervision.
Play role play, colour matching, finishing stories and turn-taking games.
Try cut-and-paste activities with safe tools, simple games with rules and outdoor movement.
Support discovery with letter-sound awareness, number matching, story building and cooperative games.
Keep track of nappy, skin and feeding records. Plan check-ups with your health team; ask about age-specific urgency for fever or feeding difficulties.
Plan teeth and mouth care with a health professional. Record growth measurements with dates; don't compare the pace of development with other children.
Do handwashing, toothbrushing and daily self-care routines together. Respect readiness when it comes to toilet habits.
Keep up with dental, hygiene, movement and routine health check-ups. Give your child age-appropriate chances to take part in their own care.
Don't leave them alone on high surfaces. Keep small parts, cables, medicines and hot drinks out of reach; use a suitable car seat.
Check stair, window, water and kitchen risks. Prepare food to reduce choking risk; supervise constantly near water.
Talk about traffic, playgrounds, water safety and boundaries with strangers in an age-appropriate way. Use suitable protective gear for cycling and similar activities.
Check vaccinations against your child's official vaccination card; notes in this app are not an official record.
Before vaccination, tell the health staff about any previous serious reactions and known allergies.
Take growth measurements, your questions and a list of medicines to the check-up appointment.
For unexpected or severe symptoms after vaccination, get support from a health facility.
Children develop at different speeds; the timing of a single skill alone doesn't mean a diagnosis.
Record new skills with dates and short observations; discuss any loss of earlier skills with a health professional.
Offer age-appropriate play, face-to-face interaction and safe spaces to move.
If you have concerns about development, talk to your paediatrician; don't assume it will pass.
Note when the symptom started, how long it lasted, any other signs and how it was measured.
Get emergency medical help for difficulty breathing, a change in consciousness or signs of serious dehydration.
Use medicines only according to age, weight and the doctor's advice.
Especially in young babies there are different urgency rules for fever by age; ask a doctor.
Record new foods, amounts and when any symptoms started.
Signs such as swelling of the face or tongue, difficulty breathing or fainting need emergency assessment.
With a suspected food allergy, don't start a long-term food restriction on your own.
Share known allergies with caregivers and health professionals.
Add the medicine name, prescribing doctor, time given and amount to the note.
This app does not calculate doses and is not a substitute for a reliable medical alarm for medicine reminders.
Don't make up for missed doses by giving double; ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice specific to the medicine.
Keep medicines in a safe place out of children's reach.
You can record the date the first tooth came through and mouth care habits.
Start cleaning teeth from the first tooth; check the right amount of fluoride toothpaste for their age with a dentist.
Falling asleep with a bottle and sugary drinks can harm dental health.
See a dentist for tooth pain, injury or a clear change in colour.
Record the appointment date, the facility and questions to ask.
Take previous test results, the medicine list and the vaccination card with you.
After the visit, note the doctor's plan in your own words.
This record doesn't provide automatic notifications or official appointment confirmation.
Adjust routines such as bathing, skin care and nappy changes to your child's needs.
Provide a safe, age-appropriate sleep environment; follow back-sleeping advice for young babies.
Keep cleaning products and small swallowable objects out of children's reach.
Note any skin irritation or other symptoms after changes in care.
Feeding in the first months
Keep breastfeeding or formula records. If you're worried about feeding difficulties, weight gain or whether it's enough, see a health professional.
Note signs of readiness for solids and new foods. A suitable texture that reduces choking risk and safe sitting are important.
Keep track of varied foods and possible reactions. Age-appropriate piece sizes and supervision are important.
Safe sleep environment
Put your baby on their back on a flat, firm sleep surface; keep loose pillows and covers out of the sleep space.
Note regular sleep and wake times; adapt the routine to your child's needs.
Supervised tummy time
Give short tummy play opportunities while your baby is awake and supervised; if they struggle, talk to a specialist.
Interactive games
Try hiding objects, looking at books together and talking games; the pace of development can vary between children.
Language and movement games
Spend time together with books, imitation, music and safe movement games.
Safety at home
Keep medicines, cleaning products and small objects out of reach. Use an age-appropriate car seat.
Check-up and vaccination records
Record the vaccination and check-up dates given by your health facility; follow current official health sources for the schedule.
Mouth and tooth care
Track teething; plan age-appropriate mouth care and the first dental check-up with a health professional.
Daily note for caregivers
Create a daily summary to safely share feeding, sleep and important care information with caregivers.

For about the first 6 months the main food is breast milk or suitable infant formula. Discuss when to start solids with a health professional.
Start solids with small amounts. Include iron-containing foods, different tastes and suitable textures. Breast milk or formula continues.
Offer increasingly varied foods and textures suited to your baby's skills. The number and size of meals is individual.
Support joining balanced family meals in an age-appropriate way. Variety, safe textures and regular meals are important.
Gentle skin cleansing
Cleanse your skin morning and evening without irritating it. Use lukewarm rather than very hot water. Apply a moisturiser suited to your skin after cleansing.
When using a new product, test it on a small area; for persistent redness, see a dermatologist.
Sun protection
Use a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen in your daily routine. Reapply outdoors according to the label; add physical measures such as shade and a hat.
Ask your doctor about ingredients during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
